title: Nonlinear formulations and improved randomized approximation algorithms for multiway and multicut problems
contribution: An exact probabilistic nonlinear formulation of multiway cut and multicut whose linearizations generate known and new LP relaxations, a reduction to stable set that yields perfect-graph integrality results, and a dependent (single-threshold) randomized rounding giving 2(1 - 1/k) and 2 alpha(H)(1 - 1/|V(H)|) bounds relative to the LP.
problem_entry: {IO; LO as engine} Multiway cut is NP-hard for k >= 3; polyhedral work (Chopra-Rao, Cunningham, Chopra-Owen) and approximation results (Dalhaus et al.; Garg-Vazirani-Yannakakis) exist separately; the entry is to derive all formulations from one exact nonlinear model and analyse the LP relaxations by rounding (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Make y_j(u) the probability that node u joins terminal j's component, so an edge is cut with probability 1 - sum_j y_j(u)y_j(v); the resulting NLP is exact (Theorem 1, p. 6); linearizations give EF1-EF3 (pp. 7-9), a stable-set view on I(G) imports clique and odd-cycle inequalities (pp. 13-17), and one shared uniform threshold rounds all nodes (pp. 18-19).
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights (from p. 8), k terminals; multicut with demand graph H and independence number alpha(H) (pp. 3, 8, 22); no data.
proof_devices: exactness of the nonlinear program by sampling a cut from its optimum (Theorem 1, p. 6)
equivalence of extended formulations by explicit feasibility maps (Theorem 3, pp. 8-9)
projection of auxiliary variables to derive path, tree, odd-wheel and bipartite inequalities (Theorem 4, pp. 9-11)
explicit fractional extreme points: gap 16/15 and a family tending to 10/9 (pp. 11-13)
reduction to maximum-weight stable set on I(G); NP-hardness of max independent set on k-partite graphs as a corollary (p. 15)
perfect-graph integrality and clique-gluing for trees and triangular cacti (Theorems 7-9, Lemma 10 sketched, pp. 17-18)
dependent randomized rounding with one uniform U; P(edge in cut) = |y_j(u) - y_j(v)|; drop the largest cut for the (1 - 1/k) factor (Theorem 11, p. 19; fraction restored from the proof)
derandomization by conditioning or threshold minimum cuts (p. 20)
randomized proof of max-flow min-cut for k = 2 (p. 19)
experiments: none (only Chopra and Owen's computations are mentioned, p. 3)
positioning: Builds on polyhedral work (Chopra-Rao, Cunningham, Chopra-Owen) and approximation results (Dalhaus et al.; Garg et al.); recovers Chopra-Owen's formulation and Erdos-Szekely's tree result as corollaries; claims only a slight improvement over Dalhaus et al. (pp. 2-3, 17-18).
writing: Numbered contribution list mapped to sections (p. 3); modest wording ('slight improvement'; multicut bound 'weaker for sparse graphs') (p. 3); short concluding remarks with no future work (p. 24).
limits_future: Bound gain over Dalhaus et al. is slight and comes from being relative to the LP (pp. 3, 20); multicut bound weaker than Garg et al. on sparse demand graphs (p. 3); Lemma 10 only sketched (p. 18); no future directions (p. 24).

method_links.note: IO problem owned by approximation algorithms and polyhedral combinatorics written exactly as a nonlinear program whose linearizations are polynomially solvable LPs; boundary printed as integrality gaps (16/15, to 10/9) and as the graph classes where the LP is integral; the Domain Map's IO 'LP-relaxation rounding'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact nonlinear (probabilistic) formulation as a generator of LP relaxations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Linearizing the products of an exact probabilistic model recovers Chopra-Owen's extended formulation and the classical multicut LP and yields stronger new ones; also S213 and S500 in this batch.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dependent randomized rounding with one shared threshold
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: One uniform U thresholds every fractional y_j(u); the cut probability equals an l1 term already in the LP; S256 (with Teo) reuses the device.

transferable: Make assignment variables probabilities, write each cost event's probability, and prove the nonlinear model exact by sampling a solution from its optimum (Theorem 1, p. 6).
Generate relaxations by linearizing the exact model's products in several ways (product variable; l1 bound), checking first that the published formulation is recovered (pp. 7-9).
Round with one shared uniform threshold so each edge's cut probability equals an LP term; drop the most expensive part to gain a (1 - 1/k) factor (pp. 18-19).
Quantify a formulation's weakness with an explicit fractional extreme point and a scalable family whose gap has a limit (pp. 11-13).

quotes.text: Compared with traditional randomized rounding, our algorithm introduces dependencies in the rounding process.
The route through the nonlinear characterization offers additional insights into the above formulation.

title: Stability conditions for multiclass fluid queueing networks
contribution: An LP test that exactly characterizes global stability of two-station multiclass fluid networks under all work-conserving policies, shown by LP duality to be equivalent to the piecewise-linear Lyapunov-function test, plus sufficient LP conditions for any number of stations.
problem_entry: {SD; LO} The load condition is not sufficient for multiclass networks with feedback (even FIFO can be unstable); Lyapunov-function LPs give only sufficient conditions, and whether piecewise-linear Lyapunov functions can be exact was open (p. 1).
key_idea: Decompose any stable trajectory into four phase types by busy stations, aggregate time and work per type into LP variables, bound the emptying time by an LP, and test stability by whether the homogeneous LP[0] has only the zero solution (Propositions 1-2, Theorems 1-3, pp. 2-7).
assumptions: Deterministic fluid model (alpha, mu, P, C) with substochastic routing of spectral radius below one, work-conserving allocations, stability as emptying in finite time, load condition rho < e; exact result for two stations only (pp. 1-2, 7).
proof_devices: trajectory decomposition by regions R1, R2, R12 into four phase types (Proposition 1, pp. 2-3)
LP bound on the strong busy period from work conservation and boundary conditions (Proposition 2, pp. 3-5)
sufficiency by contradiction: bounded LP[Q(0)] value Z, follow an unstable policy until Z then switch to a stable one (Theorem 1, p. 5)
necessity by constructing a periodic unstable trajectory from a nonzero LP[0] solution (Theorem 2, pp. 6-7)
load contradictions by multiplying with C M^-1 [I - P']^-1 (pp. 6-8)
LP duality: Down-Meyn's Lyapunov LP feasible iff its dual has only the zero solution, and that dual is equivalent to LP[0] (Lemmas 5-9, Corollary 1, pp. 9-12)
emptying-time decomposition for J stations giving G[0] with nJ variables (Theorem 10, p. 13)
experiments: none (the test is called efficiently solvable, but no instance is solved, p. 13)
positioning: Answers an open question of the Lyapunov-function line (Kumar-Meyn, Botvich-Zamyatin, Dai-Weiss, Down-Meyn) for two stations and generalizes Kumar's and Down-Meyn's three-class examples; relies on Dai's fluid-limit theorem for relevance (pp. 1, 7-8).
writing: Three numbered contributions (p. 1); the J > 2 necessity stated openly as a belief that could not be proved (pp. 1, 13); a 'special case' section to show the power of the test (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Necessity for more than two stations only conjectured; fluid-stochastic equivalence not fully proven, so no iff for stochastic networks (p. 13). An authors' correction appeared in 1997 (per 03-process-evidence.md; not read).

method_links.note: Stability, owned by the Lyapunov-function and stochastic-process tradition, becomes an LP feasibility test; the dual is read to settle the rival method's power; the boundary (J > 2 sufficient only; fluid-to-stochastic transfer unproven) is printed. Adds an LP stability device to the SD row voiced from co-authored papers only.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact region as the condition that a homogeneous LP has only the zero solution, converse by explicit periodic counterexample
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Only-zero solution gives a bounded LP and a contradiction; a nonzero solution is turned into a periodic unstable trajectory.

transferable: Turn a dynamic property into an LP by decomposing an arbitrary trajectory into phases by active constraints and aggregating time and work per phase into variables (pp. 2-5).
Prove an iff with one LP: only-zero solution gives boundedness and a contradiction; a nonzero solution yields an explicit periodic counterexample (pp. 5-7).
Compare with a rival certificate by dualizing its LP and showing the two relax each other, so exactness transfers to the rival method (pp. 8-12).

quotes.text: Using linear programming duality, we show that for two-station systems the Lyapunov function approach is equivalent to ours and therefore characterizes stability exactly.
new sufficient conditions for multiclass networks with more than two stations that we believe are necessary, although we were unable to establish necessity

title: Multiclass queueing systems in heavy traffic: an asymptotic approach based on distributional and conservation laws
contribution: Multiclass distributional laws combined with conservation laws give closed-form heavy-traffic approximations for multiclass GI/G/1 queues under FIFO, priorities and gated polling, closer to simulation than Brownian heavy-traffic formulas in most tested cases.
problem_entry: {SD} Brownian heavy-traffic limits exist for FIFO and priority queues, conservation laws give priority performance only for Poisson arrivals, and polling is solved only for Poisson arrivals; the target is multiclass systems with general renewal arrivals (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Extend the distributional law to several classes (Theorem 2, p. 3), add conservation laws and the server's state to get a complete 4N x 4N system (pp. 6-7), and solve it asymptotically with renewal-kernel expansions (Theorem 3, p. 5): heavy traffic as solving fundamental equations asymptotically (p. 1).
assumptions: Overtake-free systems: one-at-a-time arrivals and departures, FIFO within the system, no influence of later arrivals, independent renewal streams (A.1-A.4, pp. 2-3); nonarithmetic times (p. 8); priority results asymptotically exact only for subsets with load tending to 1 (p. 11); N-class nonpreemptive needs a common service distribution (pp. 9, 16).
proof_devices: random-observer and reverse-time numbering argument for the multiclass distributional law (Theorem 2, pp. 3-4)
Little's law at the server and conditioning on the class in service (pp. 6-7)
Smith's renewal asymptotics for the kernels, checked by numerical Laplace inversion with two algorithms (Theorem 3, pp. 5-6)
set function b(A) evaluated under FIFO within priority groups because it is invariant across policies that favour A (Theorem 8, pp. 9-10)
heavy-traffic decomposition of polling waits generalizing Fuhrmann-Cooper; N x N linear system for cycle-time variances (Proposition 2, Theorem 9, pp. 11-15)
experiments: Closed forms (DL) vs simulation and traditional heavy traffic (HT) on seven setups (Tables II-XII, pp. 15-18): DL usually closer, HT better for H2/M/1 with c^2 > 1 (p. 15); at rho = 0.4 one Erlang/M/1 case has DL -82% and HT +78% (Table II, p. 15); polling within about 2.2% (Table XII, p. 18); no run lengths or confidence intervals reported.
positioning: An alternative to Brownian heavy-traffic limits (Iglehart-Whitt, Fendick-Saksena-Whitt, Whitt, Reiman-Simon, Coffman et al.); extends Haji-Newell, Keilson-Servi and Bertsimas-Nakazato; generalizes Sarkar-Zangwill and the Fuhrmann-Cooper decomposition (pp. 1-2, 12).
writing: A methodological manifesto in the introduction ('physics tradition'), hedged with 'we feel' (p. 1); the numerical section is organized around three posed questions (p. 15); insights listed at the end (pp. 17-18).
limits_future: Accuracy grows with the waiting time and with closeness to Poisson arrivals: best for polling, then priority, then FIFO (pp. 17-18); weak at low load and for c^2 > 1 (p. 15); priority results approximate for classes not in heavy traffic (p. 11); no future work stated.

method_links.note: Formulation first, but as a complete equation system from general laws solved asymptotically, not a problem kept in an optimization class; the conservation-law set function (the polymatroid object behind SW1) is used as an analysis device.
Only steps 5-6: closed forms dueled against the incumbent approximation (HT) with simulation as ground truth, losing regimes printed (c^2 > 1; low load); no certificate step. Heuristic 4 evidence.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: laws-first analysis: complete equation system from general laws, solved asymptotically
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Define the random variables, derive the laws relating them for every traffic level, then treat heavy traffic as solving those equations asymptotically.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: evaluate a policy-invariant quantity under the most tractable admissible policy
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: b(A) is the same for all work-conserving nonanticipative policies favouring A, so it is computed under FIFO inside A and E - A.

transferable: Before approximating, count unknowns and laws and add laws (Little's law at the server, conservation) until the system is square; expand asymptotically only then (pp. 6-7).
If a quantity is invariant across a class of policies, compute it under the most tractable member of the class (p. 9).
Report simulation, your approximation and the incumbent approximation side by side with percentage deviations across loads, and say where the incumbent wins (Tables II-IV, pp. 15-16).

quotes.text: Heavy traffic, then, is nothing more than solving the equations that describe the system asymptotically.
It is instructive to note that for c2 < 1 or c2 ~ 1 our method slightly outperforms the HT, although things are reversed when c2 > 1.

title: A new algebraic geometry algorithm for integer programming
contribution: A Groebner-basis algorithm for 0-1 integer programs written as polynomial equalities that enumerates and counts all feasible solutions, certifies infeasibility, extends to general IP optimization and gives sensitivity analysis, illustrated on small examples.
problem_entry: {IO} Any 0-1 IP is a system of quadratic equalities (x_j^2 = x_j with Ax = b); unlike Conti-Traverso's toric approach it fixes b (like Thomas-Weismantel), linking to Nullstellensatz infeasibility proofs (Pitassi, Lovasz) (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Compute a lex-order reduced Groebner basis of <Ax - b, x_j^2 - x_j>: G = {1} certifies infeasibility, otherwise back-substitution through the elimination ideals enumerates all solutions; standard monomials count them; adding y - c'x gives the feasible costs as roots; keeping b_i as a variable gives the value function (pp. 3-10).
assumptions: Integer data; complex field so the variety equals the 0-1 feasible set (pp. 2-3); bounded variables or the Papadimitriou-Steiglitz bound; inequalities via binary slacks (p. 9); no data sets.
proof_devices: elimination and extension theorems with the Nullstellensatz for correctness of Algorithm A (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4)
count of solutions as the number of standard monomials of a radical ideal (Theorem 2, p. 6)
structural properties of the reduced basis: triangular partition, binomial and square-free groups (Properties 1-3, pp. 5-6)
Farkas-lemma reading of G = {1} as an infeasibility certificate (p. 7)
construction of an IP for a given 0-1 point set via quadratic exclusion inequalities and binary slacks (Theorem 3, p. 7)
a family where LP-based branch and bound needs exponentially many subproblems (Example 9, p. 8)
experiments: Own C implementation of Buchberger's algorithm on a PC (p. 4); 13 small examples; problems 'of up to 100 variables', faster when infeasible or with few solutions, one 100-variable example (p. 10); no timings, no solver or branch-and-bound comparison beyond an argument on Example 9 (p. 8).
positioning: Distinguished from Conti-Traverso (toric ideals over all right-hand sides) and aligned with Thomas-Weismantel's fixed-b view; inspired by Pitassi and Lovasz on Nullstellensatz proofs (p. 1).
writing: Example-driven exposition (13 examples); numbered contributions (pp. 1-2); computational claims hedged as 'preliminary' and 'shows promise' (pp. 1, 10).
limits_future: Useful mainly for infeasible problems or problems with few solutions (pp. 1, 10); no complexity bound or timings; no future directions stated (p. 10).

method_links.note: Formulation first (0-1 IP as a polynomial system), but the target is an algebraic object rather than an LP, conic or MIO class, and tractability is not measured (no solve times, no complexity bound): the case Method 1's stop rule forbids. The infeasibility certificate supports Research Taste mark 7.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact nonlinear (polynomial) formulation as a generator of relaxations and certificates
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Binary constraints as x_j^2 - x_j = 0 make the Groebner basis an enumerator, a counter and an infeasibility certificate; with S658 and S500 in this batch.

transferable: Write binary constraints as x_j^2 - x_j = 0 next to Ax - b; a lex-order reduced Groebner basis is triangular and back-substitution enumerates all solutions (pp. 3-5).
Add y - c'x to the ideal to obtain all feasible objective values as roots of a polynomial in y; keep b_i as a variable for the value function (pp. 8-10).
Read basis elements as logical implications (exactly one of two; equal pairs) to expose the feasible set's structure (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: Our results are inspired from the observation that we can view any 0–1 IP as a system of quadratic equalities.
In preliminary computational work, we have observed that Algorithm A is computationally faster, when the problem is either infeasible or it has very few solutions.

title: Probabilistic service level guarantees in make-to-stock manufacturing systems
contribution: Production policies for multiclass make-to-stock systems that minimize inventory cost subject to per-class stockout-probability guarantees, with sequencing from a fluid control problem and hedging points from large-deviations asymptotics valid for autocorrelated demand and failure-prone production.
problem_entry: {SD; AP} Linear backorder costs serve tractability and cannot be estimated from data, so service becomes stockout-probability bounds; demand and production are autocorrelated, so distributions beyond two moments matter (p. 2); minimize inventory cost subject to P(stockout_j) <= eps_j (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: Sequencing from a deterministic fluid control problem (priority by b_j or GLQF by c_j|x_j|, Proposition 5.1, pp. 5-6); idling by base-stock hedging points set from large-deviations decay rates after the make-to-order transformation L = w - x (pp. 4, 6-9); priority order chosen by an analytic inventory-cost approximation (pp. 10-11).
assumptions: Discrete time; stationary demand and production with mild mixing (renewal, Markov-modulated) (pp. 2-3); stability (p. 3); linear and quadratic costs used only for structure (p. 3); stockout fraction, not waiting, controlled (p. 3); policies not optimal for the cost objective (p. 7); GLQF asymptotics only for two classes (p. 9).
proof_devices: Gartner-Ellis large deviations and the M/M/1 exactness check theta* = mu - lambda (pp. 3-5)
Pontryagin's minimum principle for the fluid control problem, necessary and sufficient by convexity (Proposition 5.1, pp. 5-6)
make-to-stock to make-to-order transformation L = w - x, stockout = overflow probability (pp. 4, 7)
optimal-control formulation of the most likely overflow path giving a tight lower bound matched by a large-deviations upper bound (Remark 2, p. 8)
decay rate as the largest root of a convex function (Theorem 7.2, p. 8)
refined asymptotic with prefactor matched to E[L] (Abate-Choudhury-Whitt idea) to set the hedging point (eqs. 33-35, p. 9)
Kramer-Langenbach-Belz GI/G/1 approximation for E[L] under priorities (pp. 9-10)
experiments: Two synthetic Markov-modulated examples with an ON/OFF facility (three classes, priority; two classes, GLQF) (pp. 11-14): predicted best ordering matched simulation in all five cases with cost approximations within 5.5-9% (p. 11); hedging points mostly within 3% of simulated, two cases 3.8% and 7.52% partly from integer grid (p. 12); achieved stockout probabilities of the target's order (pp. 12-13); no competing-policy baseline.
positioning: Against base-stock optimality results (Evans, Sobel, Gavish-Graves, Federgruen-Zipkin), heavy-traffic and index policies (Wein; Pena Perez-Zipkin; Veatch-Wein; Ha; de Vericourt et al.) and Glasserman's renewal-only asymptotics (pp. 1-2, 6-7).
writing: Three labelled contributions, with the modelling choice argued from data availability (p. 2); the conclusion widens the claim to 'substantial performance loss' beyond what the examples measure (p. 13).
limits_future: m! search over orderings with a heuristic suggested (p. 11); E[L] needs simulation or approximation (pp. 9, 12); GLQF beyond two classes lacks asymptotics (p. 9); proposed online estimation of Markov-modulated models and policy updates (p. 12).

method_links.note: Step 3 (shape the model around the data that exist): backorder costs dropped as unestimable, inventory-cost slopes kept, online estimation proposed; but no owner's current rule as baseline and only synthetic examples.

Property = service level, knob = eps_j per class, price = hedging point; curve tabulated for eps from 0.15 to 1e-4; the knob-price relation is an asymptotic formula exact only for M/M/1, not a solution-independent bound.

A rare-event probability computed as the value of a deterministic optimal-control problem (most likely path), reduced to a largest root of a convex function; an optimization lens on probability but not an LP, conic or MIO class.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fluid model for policy structure, rare-event asymptotics for its parameters
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sequencing structure from the fluid control problem; hedging points from large-deviations decay rates.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: replace an unmeasurable penalty by a probabilistic constraint with a per-class knob
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Linear backorder costs replaced by stockout-probability bounds eps_j because backorder costs cannot be estimated.

transferable: Under a base-stock policy substitute L = w - x so the stockout probability becomes a buffer-overflow probability with known asymptotics (pp. 4, 7).
Decide the structure of a stochastic control policy in the fluid limit and tune its safety parameters with rare-event asymptotics (pp. 3, 5-9).
Calibrate an exponential tail approximation's prefactor by matching its mean to E[L], then invert it for the threshold meeting a target probability (p. 9).
Validate analytic thresholds against simulated ones over a range of targets and separate grid-quantization error from method error (p. 12).

quotes.text: The assumption of linear backorder costs, that is often made in the literature, appears to serve analytical tractability rather than an accurate representation of reality.
The important conclusion is that the optimal priority ordering may depend on subtle distributional differences between classes that cannot be captured by just the first few moments.

title: Multistage lot sizing problems via randomized rounding
contribution: A single-threshold randomized rounding that re-derives the 94% and 98% power-of-two bounds from any feasible relaxed solution, extends them to submodular ordering costs and resource constraints, and with a stronger relaxation gives a 95.8% bound for the fixed-base joint replenishment problem against dynamic policies.
problem_entry: {IO; AP} Roundy's 94%/98% guarantees depend on the EOQ structure of the relaxation's optimum and fail for merely feasible inputs (p. 4); Lu-Posner's schemes do not help the fixed-base model and the optimal policy's complexity is open (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Round all T_i = 2^p_i z_i T_L with one random Y whose distribution makes E[T_i] and E[1/T_i] grow by the same factor 1.06 (Theorem 1, p. 4); log-uniform Y recasts Roundy's 98% (p. 5); order preservation handles submodular costs (p. 5); a stronger joint-replenishment relaxation plus a mix of power-of-two and 3*2^p roundings gives 1.043 (pp. 7-9).
assumptions: Acyclic assembly or distribution network, constant demand, infinite assembly rate (zero-ordering property), holding cost at a node no larger than at its predecessors, stationary nested policies, fixed or optimized base period (pp. 1-2); no data.
proof_devices: single shared threshold with tuned distribution so expected order interval and its reciprocal are bounded by the same factor (Theorem 1, p. 4)
derandomization by enumerating at most n + 1 outcomes after sorting, O(n log n) (p. 4)
order-preserving rounding keeps the Edmonds greedy maximizer of a submodular cost optimal (Theorem 4, p. 5)
scaling by sqrt(2) to keep resource constraints feasible (Theorems 5-6, p. 6)
piecewise-linear interpolated relaxation as a lower bound on dynamic policies via convexity (Propositions 1-2, pp. 7-8)
randomized mixing of two rounding classes with p = 0.7, q = 0.3 (Theorem 7, pp. 8-9)
experiments: none (the paper does not discuss solving the relaxations efficiently in practice, p. 3)
positioning: Recasts Roundy's 98% algorithm as randomized rounding and credits his averaging argument (pp. 3-4); extends Roundy (1989) to submodular costs; improves the 94% fixed-base joint-replenishment bound where Lu-Posner's approach fails (p. 3).
writing: Simplicity declared as the main objective (p. 3); numbered contributions (p. 3); limits given as remarks after the main theorem (p. 9).
limits_future: Intervals with T* = 2 lose in rounding, which also rules out intervals of 5T_L and above (p. 9); solving relaxations efficiently not discussed (p. 3); one-warehouse multiretailer improvements deferred to Teo-Bertsimas 1996 and Teo's thesis (p. 3).

method_links.note: IO as engine: a problem owned by inventory theory handled through a convex relaxation and rounding; the improvement comes from a stronger formulation (conclusion) and the boundary (no extension to 5T_L and beyond) is printed; supports the IO row's LP-relaxation rounding and strong formulations.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dependent randomized rounding with one shared threshold
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: One random Y rounds all items, with its distribution tuned to balance ordering and holding terms; second instance after S658, both with Teo.

transferable: For costs K/T + HT choose the threshold distribution so rounding inflates T and 1/T by the same factor; one common draw keeps policies nested (p. 4).
Derandomize a single-threshold rounding by enumerating the n + 1 breakpoints of the sorted fractional parts (p. 4).
With a cost that is a maximum over a polymatroid, use order-preserving rounding so the same greedy vertex stays optimal (p. 5).
To beat a classical bound, strengthen the relaxation first, then randomize between two rounding classes and tune the mixing probability (pp. 7-9).

quotes.text: We perform a randomized rounding analysis and show that the dependence on the structure of the optimal solution can be removed for the 1.06 bound to hold.
This difficulty also precludes the possibility of extending the technique to include order intervals of type 5TL and above.

title: Geometry, moments, and semidefinite optimization
contribution: Encodes known support or geometry as Putinar-type semidefinite moment constraints, giving mesh-free SDP bounds on linear functionals of linear PDEs and tighter optimal probability bounds than moments alone.
problem_entry: {CP; SD and PDEs as applications} Geometry of the feasible set is rarely exploited; a moment relaxation over a polyhedron ignores that m must be a moment sequence with known support K, so optimize over P intersected with V(K) (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Haviland plus Putinar turn 'moment sequence on K' into PSD localizing matrices (Theorems 1-3, pp. 3-4); PDEs: weak form with monomial test functions and the adjoint gives linear moment equalities, plus PSD constraints for u - u0 >= 0 (pp. 5-8); probability: Putinar certificates in the dual of the (n, k, Omega) bound (pp. 12-13).
assumptions: Linear differential operators with polynomial coefficients, separable test-function class, compact support or exponentially decaying tails (pp. 5-6); compact basic semialgebraic K satisfying Putinar's condition, support known a priori (pp. 1-4).
proof_devices: Haviland's theorem and Putinar's Positivstellensatz giving localizing-matrix conditions (Theorems 1-3, pp. 3-4)
truncation hierarchy with worst-case exponential degree unless P = NP (p. 4)
adjoint operator by integration by parts or Stokes's formula, automatable (pp. 6, 10)
shift u - u0 >= 0 with u0 as a decision variable to impose moment constraints (p. 7)
LP duality between moment problem and polynomial nonnegativity (p. 13)
experiments: SeDuMi, SDPA, SOSTOOLS and an LP code (pp. 9, 11, 13): Bessel moment bounds tight to four decimals but min/max approximations near -0.31 and 0.50 vs true -0.347 and 0.583 (Tables 1-2, p. 10); Helmholtz LP bounds loose (+inf on m0,0) vs tight SDP bounds, times under 0.5 s to 1-3 min (Tables 3-4, pp. 11-12); SDPA instabilities (p. 11); support lowers probability bounds by up to 20-30% but not at three moments (Tables 5-6, p. 14).
positioning: Builds on Bertsimas-Popescu's optimal inequalities and Caramanis's Master's thesis; imports Haviland, Schmudgen, Putinar, Parrilo and SOSTOOLS (pp. 1-4, 13, 15).
writing: Opens with rhetorical questions about the feasible set (p. 1); 'powerful' and 'we believe' framing (pp. 1, 14-15); bound tables as evidence (pp. 10-14).
limits_future: Truncation only necessary and exponential in the worst case (p. 4); max/min only one-sided (p. 8); numerical instability (p. 11); effect of geometry setup-dependent (p. 14); future: many more applications (p. 15).

method_links.note: Probability and PDE questions become SDPs; the worst case is read from the dual (polynomial nonnegativity); the boundary is printed (truncation only necessary, exponential degree unless P = NP, one-sided max/min); matches the CP row.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact nonlinear (polynomial) formulation as a generator of relaxations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Support written as polynomial inequalities yields a hierarchy of SDP relaxations through Putinar certificates; with S658 and S213 in this batch.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: use cheap structural information before buying more data
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Support constraints at low moment order tighten bounds more cheaply than higher-order moments.

transferable: Bound a linear functional of a linear PDE without a mesh: weak form with monomial test functions, adjoint by integration by parts, linear moment equalities, then PSD constraints for u - u0 >= 0 with u0 as a variable (pp. 5-8).
Add the support's localizing matrices before adding higher-order moments; they are cheaper and can tighten more (p. 14).
Print LP-only and SDP bounds side by side to isolate the value of the geometry constraints (Tables 3-4, p. 12).

quotes.text: However, the specific details of this geometry are rarely exploited as extensively as they can, and should be exploited.

SDPA gave very tight bounds; however, there were nevertheless some numerical instabilities, which required us to change the desired accuracy in the search parameters, in order to obtain answers that made sense.
